slides: Let's continue with this question, now with psychometric thinking.

slides.say: [pause] Now the psychometric way. Our second super-method is plugging in numbers, and it's one of the most important methods for the exam. The question has two letters, a and b, and so do the choices.

If two expressions are really the same, they must give the same result for every a and b. So we pick one pair of numbers, and put it into the question and into each choice. A choice that gives a different result can't be the same expression.
at: If two expressions are really the same

slides.say: Which numbers? Easy ones, as long as we keep the condition, a and b are not zero. Let's take a equal to one. For b, I could take two, three, any number. But I can also take one again. Nobody said a and b must be different, and one is the easiest number to calculate with.
at: Let's take a equal to one

slides.say: Let's put one in for both letters. One squared is one, and the other one squared is one too. One minus one is zero, and zero squared is zero. So the top is one plus one plus zero, which is two. The bottom is two times one times one, also two. Two over two is one. Then we add the one outside the fraction, and get two.
Now the choices, with a and b equal to one. A choice that gives two could be the right one. A choice that gives anything else is out.
Choice number one says a over b, plus b over a. One over one is one, plus one over one, one. That's two. It fits, but we can't mark it yet, so we keep checking.
Choice number two says a over two b, plus b over two a. One over two is a half, plus another half, that's one. One is not two, so choice number two is out.
at: One over two is a half
so choice number two is out

slides.say: Choice number three says a plus b, times a minus b, all over a b. One minus one is zero, and zero on top makes the whole fraction zero. Zero is not two, so choice number three is out.
Choice number four says two times, a squared plus b squared. One plus one is two, and two times two is four, not two. Choice number four is out too.
Three choices are out, so we can mark choice number one.
at: so we can mark choice number one

slides.say: This is a very important point. One matching result doesn't prove a choice is right. We need to rule out the other three. A wrong expression can match by chance. For example, a plus b also gives two when both letters are one. But it isn't always equal to our expression. If two choices remain, we try another easy pair. We check the question again, and only those two choices.

So when do I plug in numbers? When there are letters in the question and letters in the choices, like here. Any allowed numbers will do, so we choose easy ones. It's a safety net for when the algebra gets tangled.
at: So when do I plug in numbers

slides.say: One more example. Two to the power of x plus one, plus two to the power of x. What is it equal to? The choices are two to the power of two x plus one, three times two to the power of x, four to the power of x, and two to the power of x plus three.
Let's take x equal to one, because small powers of two are easy. Two squared is four, plus two to the power of one, two. So the expression gives six.
at: Let's take x equal to one

slides.say: Now the choices with x equal to one. The right one must give six too. The first gives two cubed, eight, so it's out. The second gives three times two, six. It fits. The third gives four, and the fourth gives two to the power of four, sixteen. Both are out. Three are out, so the answer is three times two to the power of x. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
